steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on learning unknown intervention targets in structural causal models from data collected across multiple environments. Motivate the problem, contrast it with prior approaches, and describe our algorithm and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- SCMs, interventions, and why intervention targets can be unknown
- Problem statement and relation to prior work
- The LIT algorithm (recovery + matching phases)
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background / motivation
  - SCM: each variable = function of direct causes + exogenous noise
  - intervention = modifying causal mechanism, i.e. changing conditional distribution of variable given direct causes
  - randomized control trials: randomized interventions on target to estimate its causal effect
  - but sometimes no full control over which variables are intervened on
  - example: causal protein-signaling networks from single-cell data; drugs inhibit/activate signaling proteins; gene expression measured; targets unknown
  - intervention by unknown source -> locate source; microservices in cloud clusters vulnerable to faults (equipment failures, adversarial attacks); locate root cause = source of fault/intervention
  - data heterogeneous, from multiple domains/environments; causal mechanisms of some variables change across environments
- Problem + prior work
  - learn unknown intervention targets from collection of interventional distributions from multiple environments
  - closely related: learning equivalence class of causal graphs consistent with interventional data (related work, Section 5)
  - some methods give info on intervention targets as byproduct
  - drawbacks: limited to linear systems; huge number of conditional and invariance tests; can't handle latent confounders
- LIT (Locating Intervention Target)
  - returns observed variables that are intervention targets
  - recovery phase: contrastive learning; exogenous noises of targets recovered up to permutation + component-wise invertible transformation
  - matching phase: match recovered noises to observed variables (if any) via conditional independence (CI) tests
- Contributions
  - recovery: identifiability for noises whose distributions change; nonlinear models, exponential family noises, mild invertibility (Assumption 1 (a)), causally sufficient (no latent confounders); with latent confounders + further assumptions (Assumption 1 (b)) still possible (Proposition 1)
  - matching: LIT recovers true targets for causally sufficient systems (Theorem 1); quadratic number of CI tests vs exponential in previous work; with latent confounders returns superset + graphical characterization (Theorem 2); latent confounders may change across environments; more informative than state-of-the-art when they don't (Remark 3)
  - experiments: LIT beats previous work with latent confounders and nonlinear SCMs

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The causal relationships among a set of variables in a system can be modeled by a structural causal model (SCM), where every variable is a function of its direct causes and some exogenous noise. An intervention on a variable can be seen as modifying its causal mechanism, i.e., changing the conditional probability distribution of the intervened variable given its direct causes. In randomized control trials, randomized interventions on a target variable are used to estimate the causal effect of the target. But in some applications we may not have full control over which variables get intervened on. For example, when recovering causal protein-signaling networks from single-cell data, drugs are injected into cells to inhibit or activate some signaling proteins, and then gene expression levels are measured. The intervention targets in these experiments are unknown. Also, sometimes an intervention is done by an unknown source and we have to locate the source of the intervention in the system. For example, microservices systems in cloud clusters are vulnerable to faults like equipment failures or adversarial attacks. It is crucial to find the root cause of faulty operation in the system by identifying the source of the fault/intervention. In these examples the collected data is often heterogeneous and comes from multiple domains/environments where the causal mechanisms of some of the variables change across the environments.

In this paper, we consider the problem of learning the unknown intervention targets from a collection of interventional distributions from multiple environments. This problem is closely related to learning an equivalence class of all causal graphs that are consistent with the collected interventional data. That problem has been studied in several works (see the related work in Section 5), and some of the proposed methods also give some information about where the intervention targets are as a byproduct of the returned equivalence class. But these methods have several drawbacks, like being limited to linear systems, needing a huge number of conditional and invariance tests, or not being able to handle latent confounders in the systems (see Section 5 for more details).

- LIT (Locating Intervention Target): returns observed variables that are targets
  - recovery phase: contrastive learning, noises of targets recovered up to permutation + component-wise invertible transformation
  - matching phase: CI tests to match noises to observed variables (if any)
- contributions
  - recovery identifiability: nonlinear, exponential family, Assumption 1 (a), causally sufficient; latent confounders under Assumption 1 (b) (Proposition 1)
  - matching: Theorem 1; quadratic CI tests vs exponential in previous work; superset + graphical characterization (Theorem 2); confounders may change; more informative (Remark 3)
  - experiments: better with latent confounders and nonlinear SCMs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The causal relationships among a set of variables in a system can be modeled by a structural causal model (SCM), where every variable is a function of its direct causes and some exogenous noise. An intervention on a variable can be seen as modifying its causal mechanism, i.e., changing the conditional probability distribution of the intervened variable given its direct causes. In randomized control trials, randomized interventions on a target variable are used to estimate the causal effect of the target. But in some applications we may not have full control over which variables get intervened on. For example, when recovering causal protein-signaling networks from single-cell data, drugs are injected into cells to inhibit or activate some signaling proteins, and then gene expression levels are measured. The intervention targets in these experiments are unknown. Also, sometimes an intervention is done by an unknown source and we have to locate the source of the intervention in the system. For example, microservices systems in cloud clusters are vulnerable to faults like equipment failures or adversarial attacks. It is crucial to find the root cause of faulty operation in the system by identifying the source of the fault/intervention. In these examples the collected data is often heterogeneous and comes from multiple domains/environments where the causal mechanisms of some of the variables change across the environments.

In this paper, we consider the problem of learning the unknown intervention targets from a collection of interventional distributions from multiple environments. This problem is closely related to learning an equivalence class of all causal graphs that are consistent with the collected interventional data. That problem has been studied in several works (see the related work in Section 5), and some of the proposed methods also give some information about where the intervention targets are as a byproduct of the returned equivalence class. But these methods have several drawbacks, like being limited to linear systems, needing a huge number of conditional and invariance tests, or not being able to handle latent confounders in the systems (see Section 5 for more details).

We propose the Locating Intervention Target (LIT) algorithm, which returns the observed variables that are intervention targets. LIT has two main phases, the recovery phase and the matching phase. In the recovery phase, we use a contrastive-learning approach to recover the exogenous noises that correspond to intervention targets, up to some permutation and component-wise invertible transformation. In the matching phase, the recovered exogenous noises are matched to the observed variables they correspond to (if there are any) by doing conditional independence (CI) tests. The main contributions of this paper are:

- For the recovery phase, we give identifiability results for recovering the exogenous noises whose distributions change across the environments. In particular, for nonlinear causal models with exogenous noises from an exponential family, recovery is possible under a mild invertibility assumption (Assumption 1 (a)) for causally sufficient systems (i.e., systems with no latent confounders). For systems with latent confounders, we show that recovery is still possible under some further assumptions (Assumption 1 (b)) (Proposition 1).

- For the matching phase, we prove that the LIT algorithm recovers the true intervention targets for causally sufficient systems using the recovered exogenous noises (Theorem 1). LIT only needs a quadratic number of CI tests. Previous work, in comparison, needed an exponential number of CI/invariance tests in the number of variables in the system. When there are latent confounders, we show that LIT returns a superset of the true intervention targets, and we give a graphical characterization of the output of recovery (Theorem 2). Different from previous work, LIT allows latent confounders to change across environments. Also, in the setting studied in the literature (i.e., when latent confounders do not change across environments), our recovery output is more informative than the state-of-the-art (see Remark 3 for more details).

- Our experiments show that LIT does better than previous work at recovering intervention targets when there are latent confounders and also when the underlying SCM is nonlinear.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Causal relationships among a set of variables in a system can be modeled by a structural causal model (SCM) where each variable is a function of its direct causes and some exogenous noise. An intervention on a variable can be considered as modifying its causal mechanism, i.e., changing the conditional probability distribution of the intervened variable given its direct causes. In randomized control trials, randomized interventions on a target variable are used to estimate the causal effect of the target. However, in some applications, we may not have full control over which variables are intervened on. For instance, in recovering causal protein-signaling networks from single-cell data [1,2], drugs are injected into cells to inhibit or activate some signaling proteins, and gene expression levels are measured. In these experiments, the intervention targets are unknown. Moreover, in some cases an intervention is done by an unknown source, and we must locate the source of the intervention in the system. As an example, microservices systems in cloud clusters are vulnerable to faults such as equipment failures or adversarial attacks, and it is crucial to locate the root cause of faulty operation by identifying the source of fault/intervention [3,4,5]. In these examples, the collected data is often heterogeneous and is gathered from multiple domains/environments where the causal mechanisms of some of the variables change across the environments.

In this paper, we consider the problem of learning the unknown intervention targets from a collection of interventional distributions obtained from multiple environments. This problem is closely related to learning an equivalence class of all causal graphs consistent with the collected interventional data. The latter problem has been studied in several works (see the related work in Section 5), and some of the proposed methods also provide some information about the locations of intervention targets as a byproduct of the returned equivalence class. These previous methods have several drawbacks, such as being limited to linear systems, requiring a huge number of conditional and invariance tests, or lacking the ability to handle latent confounders (see Section 5 for more details).

We propose the Locating Intervention Target (LIT) algorithm, which returns the observed variables that are intervention targets. LIT has two main phases: the recovery phase and the matching phase. In the recovery phase, the exogenous noises corresponding to intervention targets are recovered through a contrastive-learning approach, up to some permutation and component-wise invertible transformation. In the matching phase, the recovered exogenous noises are matched to their corresponding observed variables (if any) by performing conditional independence (CI) tests. The main contributions of this paper are:

- \bullet For the recovery phase, we provide identifiability results for recovering the exogenous noises whose distributions change across the environments. In particular, in nonlinear causal models with exogenous noises from an exponential family, the recovery is possible under a mild invertibility assumption (Assumption 1 (a)) for causally sufficient systems (i.e., there are no latent confounders). For systems with latent confounders, we show that under some further assumptions (Assumption 1 (b)) the recovery is still possible (Proposition 1).

- \bullet For the matching phase, we prove that the LIT algorithm recovers the true intervention targets for causally sufficient systems using the recovered exogenous noises (Theorem 1). LIT requires merely a quadratic number of CI tests. In comparison, previous work of [6] required an exponential number of CI/invariance tests with respect to the number of variables in the system. In the presence of latent confounders, we show that LIT returns a superset of the true intervention targets and present a graphical characterization of the output of recovery (Theorem 2). Unlike previous work, LIT allows latent confounders to change across environments. Moreover, for the setting studied in the literature (i.e., when latent confounders do not change across environments), our recovery output is more informative than the state-of-the-art (see Remark 3 for more details).

- \bullet Our experimental results show that LIT outperforms previous work in recovering intervention targets in the presence of latent confounders as well as when the underlying SCM is nonlinear.
